how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Pest control bid calculator

How much should I charge for pest control?

House size is not the cost driver on a pest control route stop — stations and drive time are. A 2,000 sq ft house with eight rodent stations and a 22-minute drive is not the same stop as an exterior spray next door with no stations at all, even at the same square footage. A 22-minute one-way drive is 44 minutes on every visit, and on a quarterly $80 account that can be more than a third of the stop.

Open the free pest control bid calculator

What a per-square-foot price cannot see

Station count. Rodent and insect stations are materials and install labor, not proportional to house size. Eight stations on a small lot can cost more than none on a bigger one.

Drive time. Doubled every visit, a long drive quietly halves the hourly rate a route stop actually pays — and it doesn't show up unless it's in the quote.

The free-initial trap. Station installs and knockdown spray on a first visit often cost more than a whole year of recurring profit on a cheap quarterly. Giving that away only works if later stops can recover it.

A bid you can defend

  1. Time the work on the lot by service type, not by house size.
  2. Add the one-way drive both ways, not just to the site.
  3. Add chemicals and station materials as their own line.
  4. Load wage burden and overhead, then price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin) for both the initial and recurring visits.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It is not a treatment recommendation, a product label, or a guarantee of control — verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and product labels before relying on it or submitting a bid.

Worked example

A 2,000 sq ft house with eight rodent stations and a 22-minute one-way drive: 44 minutes of drive time on every visit, plus station materials up front, against a quarterly $80 account. The drive alone can be more than a third of that stop's billable time. If the initial visit is offered free, the calculator reports exactly how many later quarterly visits it takes to recover the station and labor cost that first stop carried — a number worth knowing before the discount goes out.

Common questions

How do I price a pest control route stop?

Time the work on the lot, add the drive both ways, add chemicals and station materials, then load wage burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. House size is not the cost driver — stations and drive time are.

Why does drive time change a pest control bid?

A 22-minute one-way drive is 44 minutes on every visit. On a quarterly $80 account that is often more than a third of the stop, which is why the hourly rate with drive is the number to check before you accept the house.

Should I give away the initial pest control treatment?

Only if later stops can recover the first-visit cost. Station installs and knockdown spray often cost more than a whole year of recurring profit on a cheap quarterly. This calculator reports how many later visits it takes.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, product labels, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. vs-a-flat-quote-by-house-size.html.text:
← Pest Control Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat quote by house size

Pest control accounts are shopped by a flat quarterly rate tied to house size. That rate cannot see the stop — rodent stations, interior work, and drive time do not scale with square footage, and an eight-station account can take half again as long as a plain exterior spray next door.

What a flat quote by house size is

A rate by house size is the fastest number to give over the phone: hear the square footage or bedroom count, read back a quarterly price. It is also the unit homeowners already compare between competing bids, because every competitor quotes the same way.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific stop — a given set of services, station count, and drive — and then reused for the next house of that size that calls in, whether or not that next stop shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each service on the stop with its on-site minutes and material cost, rodent and insect station counts, one-way drive time, and your own wage, payroll burden, vehicle cost, overhead, and target margin. It prices the stop as its own hours and cost lines — for what is actually on the route, not a rate carried over from a house of the same size.

What a flat house-size rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for an exterior-only spray and an eight-station rodent account at the same size house, even though stations are most of the difference. Prices each service's on-site minutes and material separately, so eight rodent stations add real hours, not a guess.
Has no line for interior crack-and-crevice work versus exterior-only — both get the same house-size rate. Prices interior and exterior services as their own line items.
Has no line for drive time at all, even though a 22-minute one-way drive is 44 minutes on every visit. Prices the round-trip drive into every recurring visit and reports the effective hourly rate once it is included.
Bills every frequency the same way, with no line for how many visits it takes to recover a waived initial treatment. Reports the initial and recurring invoice separately and how many later visits recover a waived initial.
Gives the technician a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the recurring price and the break-even cost alongside it, so a house-size rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same size house, two different stops

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $20 hourly wage, 30% burden, $8 vehicle cost per visit, 15% overhead, 25% target margin, a 22-minute one-way drive, billed quarterly:

An exterior-only perimeter spray takes 1.03 crew-hours with the drive, costs $45.27 to run, and this calculator prices the recurring visit at $60.36 — $241.45 a year.

An eight-station rodent account at a similar-sized house — the same exterior spray, plus eight bait stations to check every visit — takes 1.57 crew-hours, costs $77.32 to run, and this calculator prices it at $103.09 — $412.36 a year. Quoting the rodent account at the exterior-only house-size rate of $60.36 a visit is $16.96 below that visit's own break-even cost — before counting the $170.92 it falls short of this calculator's own annual price at a 25% target margin. Same-size house, roughly half again the crew time, and a rate learned on the exterior-only stop loses money the moment eight stations are added.

Common questions

Why does a flat quote by house size get a pest control bid wrong?

Because house size only measures the building's footprint, not what the stop actually takes to run. An exterior-only spray at a house takes about 1.03 crew-hours with the drive. An eight-station rodent account at a similar-sized house next door -- same exterior spray, plus eight bait stations to check every visit -- takes about 1.57 crew-hours, roughly half again as long, because stations and interior work do not scale with square footage.

What does a flat quote by house size usually miss?

Which services are actually on the stop, how many rodent or insect stations there are, and the drive. A flat house-size rate has no line for eight stations versus zero, no line for interior crack-and-crevice work versus exterior-only, and no line for a 22-minute one-way drive that is 44 minutes on every visit -- often more than a third of a short stop.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: an exterior-only spray costs $45.27 to run per recurring visit and this calculator prices it at $60.36 -- $241.45 a year on a quarterly account. An eight-station rodent account at a similar-sized house costs $77.32 per visit to run and prices at $103.09 -- $412.36 a year. Quoting the rodent account at the exterior-only house-size rate of $60.36 a visit is $16.96 below that visit's own break-even cost, and $170.92 a year short of this calculator's price at a 25% target margin -- before the operator has done a single free station install.

Is a flat quote by house size ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar stops -- the same services and roughly the same drive as the account the rate was learned on -- a house-size number can land close. The risk is quoting a station-heavy or interior account the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know which services are on the stop or how far the drive is until the route is built, and by then the house-size number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or chemical costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's chemical and station pricing. It takes each service's on-site minutes and material cost, station counts, one-way drive time, and your own wage, payroll burden, vehicle cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew-hours and a price for this stop -- the arithmetic a flat house-size rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Pest Control Bid Calculator to price your own stop, or read how much to charge for pest control.

No warranty. This free tool is not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a treatment is compliant. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and material costs, and against a qualified professional and your state's pest control licensing board, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-pestpac.html.text:
← Pest Control Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. PestPac

Two different shapes: PestPac is an account-based platform for running a pest control company's whole operation, including scheduling and billing a route stop once it is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this stop cost, before you offer it to the customer.

What each tool is for

PestPac, sold by WorkWave, is a field service management platform built specifically for pest control businesses, from single-truck operators to national multi-branch companies. It is used to run CRM and customer records, scheduling and routing, billing and payments, marketing, reporting, and a technician mobile app, tied to one account used on an ongoing paid basis across every stop the company runs. PestPac's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that scheduling and billing software describe running, routing and invoicing a stop once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a new stop should cost from station counts, on-site minutes and drive time before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what PestPac does. It does not store a customer record, build a route across a season, or invoice anyone. It takes one stop's services — each one's on-site minutes, its rodent or insect station count, and its material cost — plus one-way drive time, service frequency, technician wage, payroll burden, vehicle cost, overhead and target margin, and turns that into the initial invoice, the recurring invoice, the hourly rate once drive time is inside it, the walk-away recurring price, and how many later visits it takes to recover a waived initial — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to store customer records, build routes, and bill customers for pest control stops across my whole business.PestPac, or a comparable field service platform — running that ongoing operation is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this stop, given its stations, on-site minutes, drive time, and my wage, burden and overhead?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How much does a 22-minute drive really cost me on a stop that looks fine priced per visit?This calculator's hourly rate with drive included.
Should I waive the initial treatment to win the house?This calculator's recovery count — how many recurring visits it takes to earn the free initial back.
I already have stops priced and need to route, bill and renew them across many customers, on a schedule, over a season.PestPac — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a per-stop pest control price actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. PestPac's tools are used through a paid account.

Most pest control businesses get different value from each: PestPac (or a comparable field service platform) for running customers, routes and billing across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what a new stop should cost before it is offered. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a signed proposal, an invoice, or a treatment guarantee.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or PestPac?

They do different jobs, and a pest control company of any size will likely end up touching both. PestPac is a field service management platform built for pest control businesses and sold by WorkWave as an ongoing subscription, used to run CRM and customer records, scheduling and routing, billing and payments, marketing, and a technician mobile app across a whole operation. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a route stop's services, each one's on-site minutes, rodent and insect station counts and material cost, plus one-way drive time, technician wage, payroll burden, vehicle cost, overhead and target margin, and turns that into the initial invoice, the recurring invoice, the hourly rate once drive time is inside it, and how many later visits it takes to recover a waived initial, before you have quoted anything. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A company already scheduling routes and billing customers across many stops is better served by PestPac or a comparable field service platform; an operator who needs an instant, private answer to what one stop should cost before it is offered is in the right place here.
